name: Roswell Incident
description: The 1947 recovery of debris from a ranch near Corona, New Mexico, by personnel from Roswell Army Air Field, briefly described in an RAAF press release as a 'flying disc' before being officially identified as a weather balloon. From the late 1970s onward, popular UFO literature reframed the recovery as the crash of an extraterrestrial vehicle and the foundation of a long-running US government cover-up.
full_description: In early July 1947, rancher William 'Mac' Brazel found scattered debris on the J. B. Foster sheep ranch near Corona, in Lincoln County, New Mexico. After hearing radio reports of 'flying discs', Brazel reported the find to Sheriff George Wilcox of Chaves County, who notified Roswell Army Air Field. Major Jesse Marcel and Captain Sheridan Cavitt examined the debris on 7 July. On 8 July 1947 the RAAF public information officer, 1st Lt. Walter Haut, issued a press release stating that the field had recovered a 'flying disc'. Within hours, Eighth Air Force commander Brigadier General Roger Ramey publicly reidentified the material as a weather balloon, and the story disappeared from the news. The incident attracted little attention until the late 1970s, when ufologist Stanton Friedman interviewed Marcel (1978) and Charles Berlitz and William Moore published The Roswell Incident (1980), reframing the recovery as an extraterrestrial event. The 1994 GAO investigation prompted the US Air Force to release reports in 1994 (The Roswell Report: Fact vs. Fiction in the New Mexico Desert) and 1997 (The Roswell Report: Case Closed) identifying the debris as Flight 4 of Project Mogul — a classified high-altitude balloon train designed to detect Soviet nuclear tests — and identifying secondary 'alien body' accounts as conflations with parachute-test dummies dropped between 1953 and 1959. Roswell remains the foundational case of modern UFO conspiracy literature and supports a substantial tourism economy in Roswell, New Mexico.

aliases.name: Foster Ranch Incident
aliases.meaning: After the Foster sheep ranch on which the debris was found

origin: The debris field is on the J. B. Foster sheep ranch in Lincoln County, New Mexico, roughly 75 miles north-west of the city of Roswell. Secondary 'crash sites' and 'body recovery' sites have been claimed at multiple locations across south-central New Mexico in later literature, with no contemporaneous physical evidence.

etymology.origin: Named for Roswell Army Air Field, the army installation whose press release made the case famous, located south of Roswell, Chaves County, New Mexico. The actual debris field is on the Foster ranch near Corona, roughly 75 miles north-west of the city.
etymology.meaning: Place-name; Roswell, New Mexico, is named for early settler Roswell Smith.

timeline.event: NYU / Project Mogul Flight 4 launched from Alamogordo Army Air Field
timeline.significance: Likely physical source of the recovered debris
timeline.source: USAF (1997), The Roswell Report: Case Closed

timeline.event: Kenneth Arnold reports nine crescent-shaped objects near Mount Rainier; press coins 'flying saucer'
timeline.significance: Sets the cultural context for the Roswell press response

timeline.event: RAAF public information officer 1st Lt. Walter Haut issues a press release stating that the field has recovered a 'flying disc'; the Roswell Daily Record runs the headline 'RAAF Captures Flying Saucer On Ranch in Roswell Region'
timeline.significance: Origin of the case in the public record
timeline.source: Roswell Daily Record (1947-07-08); RAAF press release

timeline.event: Brigadier General Roger Ramey, commander of the Eighth Air Force, holds a press conference identifying the debris as a weather balloon and Rawin radar target
timeline.significance: Effective end of the original 1947 story
timeline.source: Fort Worth Star-Telegram (1947-07-09); Ramey office photographs

timeline.event: Ufologist Stanton Friedman interviews retired Major Jesse Marcel about the 1947 recovery
timeline.significance: Catalyses the modern revival of the case
timeline.source: Friedman, S. T., Crash at Corona (1992)

timeline.event: Charles Berlitz and William Moore publish The Roswell Incident
timeline.significance: First book-length popular argument that the debris was an alien craft and that the recovery was covered up
timeline.source: Berlitz, C. & Moore, W. L. (1980), The Roswell Incident

timeline.event: The 'Majestic-12' documents are mailed to Jaime Shandera; later judged a hoax by FBI and academic analysts
timeline.significance: Conspiracy-document offshoot of the Roswell narrative
timeline.source: Federal Bureau of Investigation files; Klass, P. J. (1990), The MJ-12 Crashed-Saucer Documents

timeline.event: Kevin Randle and Donald Schmitt publish UFO Crash at Roswell
timeline.significance: Major second-generation Roswell book; Randle later changed positions on details
timeline.source: Randle, K. D. & Schmitt, D. R. (1991), UFO Crash at Roswell

timeline.event: US General Accounting Office releases its report on Roswell records, completing a request by Congressman Steven Schiff
timeline.significance: Triggers the US Air Force's first comprehensive Roswell investigation

timeline.event: USAF publishes The Roswell Report: Fact vs. Fiction in the New Mexico Desert, identifying the debris as Project Mogul Flight 4
timeline.significance: Official US government identification of the debris
timeline.source: United States Air Force (1995), The Roswell Report: Fact vs. Fiction in the New Mexico Desert

timeline.event: Ray Santilli releases 'alien autopsy' footage in London
timeline.significance: Major Roswell-adjacent hoax; Santilli admitted in 2006 it was a reconstruction
timeline.source: Santilli (2006) statement; The Real Roswell Alien Autopsy (2006 documentary)

timeline.event: USAF publishes The Roswell Report: Case Closed, identifying secondary 'alien body' accounts as conflations with high-altitude parachute-test dummies dropped 1953–1959
timeline.significance: Official US government explanation of the body-recovery accounts
timeline.source: United States Air Force (1997), The Roswell Report: Case Closed

related.name: Majestic-12
related.description: Hoaxed documents purporting to detail a US committee on Roswell crash retrieval

related.name: Kenneth Arnold sighting
related.description: 1947 Mount Rainier sighting that originated the term 'flying saucer' two weeks before Roswell

cultural_notes: Roswell is the foundational case of post-1947 American UFO conspiracy belief and continues to anchor much of the genre.
